paragraphs.source_en: Invariably tensions arose, as fathers strove to pass on as much as they could to their sons, disregarding their other relatives. After Rudolf’s death in 1368, his two brothers proved incapable of working together in the manner laid down, and ten years later they partitioned the Habsburg lands between themselves. A further division was made in 1406, with the consequence that the split now became three-way. Then in the 1450s, even the core territory of the duchy of Austria was partitioned into what became Upper and Lower Austria, divided along the line of the River Enns. Assigned to separate dukes, they were initially called ‘Austria on this side of the Enns’ and ‘Austria on the other side of the Enns.’ In order to maintain parity, the Old Fort in Vienna was also split up, with the floors assigned to separate heirs.

paragraphs.source_en: The Habsburgs might treat their possessions as private property, to be distributed and divided up as they saw fit, but this was not the opinion of their subjects. Lordship generated a sense of political community, and in each of the Habsburg lands government encountered organizations that voiced the interests of the governed. From the late fourteenth century onwards, these political communities held their own assemblies or diets, where they debated policy with the ruler and claimed increasing rights over the raising of taxes. In disputes over the succession, the diets often intervened to force agreement, appointing committees to arbitrate the contending claims.

paragraphs.source_en: Generally, diets were composed of four estates or ‘status groups’—great lords, who besides being large landowners had the right to execute maldoers; noblemen, who had less authority and usually less land, and representatives of the clergy and of the towns. Each province developed differently. In Carinthia, the lordly estate consisted in the mid-fifteenth century of only two persons, but elsewhere it was usually about a dozen; in the Tyrol, peasants attended the diet; in Habsburg Alsace, only the towns and minor noblemen were originally represented, and so on. It was a constant problem that townsfolk and peasants bought noble properties, after which they passed themselves off as noblemen. Sometimes, the diets of several or more provinces met together. In the duchy of Austria, however, the diet split into two, following the separation of the province into two halves.2
